items.claim: "Red has come up six times in a row, so black is due."
items.explanation: Independent trials have no memory. Note the mirror-image error is equally common — concluding that red is "hot" and will continue — and both come from expecting short runs to look like long-run averages.

items.claim: "His argument commits a fallacy, so his conclusion is false."
items.explanation: A bad argument for a claim leaves the claim exactly where it was — unsupported, not refuted. This is the failure mode a fallacy taxonomy itself invites, which is why it belongs in one.

items.claim: "An image of a politician shows perfectly circular pupils, but the light reflections in the left and right eyes depict completely different room window angles and shapes."
items.explanation: Diffusion generators render each eye independently, frequently failing physics-based specular ray alignment.

items.claim: Six months before any content appears, an operator buys expired domains whose names resemble regional newspapers and lets them sit dormant.
options: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution
items.explanation: Asset creation and ageing happen in the Prepare phase, long before anything is seeded — dormancy is the point, since domain age is a trust signal. Target profiling is the neighbouring Plan-phase activity and would involve studying an audience rather than building infrastructure.

items.claim: A statistic travels with the caption "crime doubled under the current mayor." What is the SIFT Trace move for this number?
options: Find a criminologist's general opinion of crime statistics
Search for other posts using the same caption to see how widely it has already traveled
Locate the original dataset or report and compare its actual finding to the caption
Check whether the poster has shared crime stories before
items.explanation: Tracing means reaching the primary source — the dataset or report — and diffing what it says against what the caption says. Echoes, poster history, and generic expert opinion do not recover the original context.

items.claim: "This procedure has been standard practice in the guild for two hundred years. That is reason enough to keep it."
items.explanation: Age is offered in place of evidence of effectiveness. Note that longevity is weak evidence rather than none — a practice that survived two centuries of use may work — but "it is old" is not the same claim as "it works", and only the second is being defended.

items.claim: Before evaluating an exposé from "Health Freedom Daily," which question belongs to SIFT's Investigate step?
options: How many shares and comments does the exposé have?
Does the exposé cite an official-sounding agency?
Who funds this outlet and what has it published that checked out or didn't?
Is the exposé's central claim emotionally persuasive enough that readers will finish it?
items.explanation: SIFT's source investigation is about funding and track record — provenance and reliability. Popularity, emotional pull, and official-sounding citations are exactly the cues the step tells you to look past.

items.claim: An investigator convinced the fire was arson spends the afternoon interviewing neighbours who reported seeing someone near the building, and never contacts the electrician who serviced the panel that week.
items.explanation: The search itself is shaped by the hypothesis — disconfirming evidence is not rejected, it is never gathered. That selective-search step is what separates it from the availability heuristic, where evidence comes to mind unbidden rather than being sought out.

items.claim: A video's caption insists a doctor said vaccines cause autism. What is SIFT's Find Better Coverage move here?
options: Read the video's description for cited papers
Watch several more videos from the same channel to check whether its claims are internally consistent
Open new tabs and see what health agencies and independent outlets say about the claim
Ask the uploader for their sources in the comments
items.explanation: Find Better Coverage is lateral reading: leave the page, consult better-placed sources on the same claim. Staying within the uploader's ecosystem or their own citations is vertical reading.

items.claim: A negotiator opens with a figure far above any plausible settlement. The final agreement lands well above what either side privately expected.
items.explanation: The opening number does not need to be credible to work; it only needs to be first. Framing is the neighbour — that would require the same value described differently, whereas here a single irrelevant number drags the whole scale.

items.claim: One outlet reports "the council seized the land"; another reports "the council acquired the land". The legal process described is identical.
items.explanation: The verb imports a verdict before any argument is made. It differs from equivocation in that no term shifts meaning WITHIN an argument — the word choice smuggles the conclusion in at the start.

items.claim: Thousands of low-quality posts on an unrelated topic bury a damaging story in every relevant feed within hours.
options: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution
items.explanation: Nothing is argued and nothing is denied — attention is simply displaced. A Gish gallop floods a DEBATE with claims; this floods a channel with noise, and needs no engagement with the story at all.

items.claim: "Either you support an immediate 100% military embargo on all trade with our neighboring rival, or you are a traitor who hates our homeland."
items.explanation: Artificially reduces a complex foreign policy spectrum to two extreme binaries while ignoring diplomatic nuances.

items.claim: A debate on whether a bridge is structurally sound is staged between a structural engineer and a local columnist, introduced as "two views".
items.explanation: The pairing implies comparable standing on a question where it does not exist. Appeal to false authority is the near miss and would apply if the COLUMNIST'S credentials were being cited as support; here the fallacy is committed by the framing, not by either speaker.

items.claim: A platform deletes 200 coordinated accounts, and the operator's next move is a post claiming "they're censoring the truth — see for yourself." What did the countermeasure risk doing?
options: Failing to measure the campaign's reach before and after the takedown
Amplifying the narrative by feeding a censorship story
items.explanation: Visible takedowns can be converted into evidence of suppression, amplifying the very narrative they targeted — the proportionality and blowback awareness the countermeasure skill trains.

items.claim: A photograph has no C2PA manifest at all.
options: This indicates the image is synthetic
This proves the metadata was stripped deliberately
This is not evidence of tampering
This indicates the image was manipulated
items.explanation: The overwhelming majority of images ever made carry no manifest, and ordinary pipelines — screenshots, messaging apps, re-encodes — strip them routinely. Treating absence as suspicion would flag almost every real photograph in existence.

items.claim: "The transport committee proposed a 15 km/h speed reduction outside primary schools. So they think cars are evil and want us all walking to work in the rain."
items.explanation: The actual proposal — a limited speed change near schools — is replaced by an absurd one that is easier to attack. This is not a slippery slope: no chain of consequences is claimed, the position itself has been swapped out.

items.claim: A driver cut off in traffic mutters "what a selfish idiot". When he does the same thing an hour later, it is because he is late for a hospital appointment.
items.explanation: Others' behaviour is explained by character, one's own by circumstance. The asymmetry is the diagnostic feature — either explanation alone could be reasonable; holding both at once is not.

items.claim: "A commercial PR firm deploys 5,000 bot accounts to coordinate posts praising a new luxury car model, making it appear like a genuine grassroots viral trend."
items.explanation: Orchestrating an artificial marketing campaign masked as spontaneous, grassroots citizen consensus.

items.claim: In a ninety-second answer, a speaker makes nineteen separate factual assertions, four of which are false and none of which the opponent has time to address.
items.explanation: The asymmetry between assertion cost and refutation cost is the weapon; the individual claims barely matter. A red herring diverts to ONE other topic, which is a different and much cheaper attack to answer.

items.claim: A friend sends you a video captioned "They don't want you to see this!" Your hands are already typing a reply. What is the SIFT-correct first move?
options: Watch the video again frame by frame for editing artifacts
Quote-tweet it with a question mark to test the reaction
Forward it to a group chat and ask whether anyone there thinks it looks fake
Pause and notice the urgency pull before doing anything else
items.explanation: STOP is the first SIFT move: noticing the emotional hook and pausing precedes every investigation step. Sharing to test reactions amplifies the claim; frame analysis skips the pause.

items.claim: "Both people I know who took that job quit within a year. It is clearly a terrible employer."
items.explanation: A sample of two is generalised to an employer of unknown size. Anecdotal evidence is the close neighbour and would be the better answer if the anecdote were being used AGAINST statistics; here there are no statistics in play, only an over-broad leap.

items.claim: "Of course the theory is only a theory — so it is hardly established fact."
items.explanation: The technical sense of "theory" — an explanatory framework supported by evidence — is swapped for the colloquial "guess". Note that the sentence contains no false statement, which is why equivocation is so much harder to answer than a lie.

items.claim: After a week of coverage of a shark attack, beach visitors rate swimming as more dangerous than the drive to the coast.
items.explanation: Ease of recall stands in for frequency, and coverage drives recall. Base-rate neglect is arguably also present, but the ENGINE is vividness and repetition — which is precisely what makes this exploitable by whoever controls the volume.
